sections.title: Identification
sections.text: Hygrophorus hypothejus is a small to medium-sized mushroom with a cap 2–6 cm across, initially convex then flattening and sometimes becoming depressed at the centre. The surface is very viscid in wet weather, yellow to olive-yellow or olive-brown, often darkest at the disc and paler toward the margin. Yellow-gold to orange stains may develop as the fruitbody ages.

sections.title: Gills, stem and flesh
sections.text: The gills are thick, waxy and rather widely spaced, pale at first then yellowish to orange, and run down the stem. The stem is pale to yellow and viscid, especially toward the base; a slimy veil may leave a fleeting ring zone that is not always apparent. The flesh is pale, sometimes yellow beneath the cap skin. Sources describe yellow-orange staining with age, but do not substantiate the previous entry’s claim that the flesh turns orange-red when bruised.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: This species is ectomycorrhizal mainly with pines, especially Scots pine. It fruits on the ground in conifer woods, often among needle litter and on poor sandy soils. Fruiting is late in the year: autumn to early winter, usually October to January in Dutch records, sometimes after the first frosts.

sections.title: Edibility and caution
sections.text: The German and Austrian mycological societies list the species as edible. This does not identify a specimen: never eat a wild mushroom based only on an image or this profile.

traits: Cap 2–6 cm across, convex then flattening and sometimes depressed, very viscid, olive-yellow to olive-brown with an often darker centre
Thick, waxy, rather widely spaced gills, pale at first then yellow to orange, decurrent
Pale to yellow stem, viscid especially toward the base; a fleeting slimy ring zone may occur
Pale flesh, sometimes yellow beneath the cap skin; yellow-orange staining may appear with age
Ectomycorrhizal mainly with pines, especially Pinus sylvestris
On the ground in conifer woods; late autumn to early winter, sometimes after the first frosts
safetyNote: The German and Austrian mycological societies list Hygrophorus hypothejus as edible. An edibility list does not confirm a specimen’s identity: do not eat a wild mushroom based only on a photo. If symptoms occur after ingestion, contact a poison centre or emergency services immediately.
